source.title: From Words to Worlds: Compositionality for Cognitive Architectures

record.file_problem: Minor PDF/OCR artifacts, but the full paper and appendices are present and readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares downstream compositional-task performance across model sizes using task accuracy and representation-based accuracy, rather than measuring held-out cross-entropy loss or fitting scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. as background; their reported results are not this study's results. It reports task outcomes across models and sizes, not held-out pretraining loss, loss-law fits, or compute-optimal allocations.
record.test_reason: Within-family size comparisons on ANTAILS and PLANE test the scale-improvement component of V6 in adjective–noun compositional reasoning. They do not establish quantitative predictability. COMPCOMB measures representation geometry rather than downstream task performance; instruction-tuning comparisons hold size fixed.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that scaling often improves compositional behavior and representations, whereas instruction tuning does not consistently do so. They suggest compositionality may explain some scaling-related performance gains, but do not directly establish that explanation or fit a downstream scaling law. Their broad statements about scaling have exceptions in their own tables, notably CodeLlama on PLANE and Mixtral's embedding-layer COMPCOMB result.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates task accuracy and representations on compositionality benchmarks across existing model checkpoints; it does not reproduce held-out-loss scaling-law measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary across task dataset, task setup, adjective class, model family, and representation layer. The authors report similar trends across the two prompt choices for ANTAILS and PLANE; COMPCOMB results differ between embedding-layer and last-hidden-state representations.

fits_no_version.finding: COMPCOMB compares cosine distances among noun, compositional-compound, and exocentric-compound representations. Larger models generally score higher, but Mixtral's embedding-layer score decreases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Semantic representation geometry often distinguishes compositional from exocentric compounds better in larger models, with layer-dependent exceptions.

fits_no_version.finding: Instruction tuning changes ANTAILS accuracy inconsistently at fixed model size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Instruction tuning does not consistently improve adjective–noun entailment performance.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the Large Language Models and Cognition Workshop, 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, Vienna, 2024
record.problems: The study focuses on adjective–noun compositionality and notes that this may provide a limited view of overall model abilities. It reports no pretraining-loss measurements or quantitative predictive fits. COMPCOMB table values have no uncertainty estimates; the authors also note the lack of error analysis and interpretability analysis.
record.rows_left_out: To remain within the 60-row limit, the PLANE tables' results for Falcon, Llama, Mistral, and Mixtral were omitted; only the CodeLlama 7B/13B comparisons across all listed adjective classes and both setups were retained (Tables 3–4). The remaining PLANE model-level results are not included.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss and power-law dependence on parameters, tokens, or compute.
Loss prediction for much larger runs from small-run fits.
Fixed-compute optimization of parameter and token allocations.
Controlled architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Power-law forms beyond text pretraining; instruction-tuned checkpoints alone do not test such forms.
Quantitative prediction rules, extrapolation, dependence on pretraining loss, and downstream domains beyond adjective–noun reasoning.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: Assessment uses only the supplied text. Tables 1–5 match the extracted numerical values. The ± quantities summarize prompt variation and should not be treated as established confidence intervals or significance tests. Other PLANE results are explicitly declared in rows_left_out, so they are not listed as missing. Layer sensitivity in COMPCOMB and prompt sensitivity in task accuracy do not themselves test V7's dependence of fitted scaling laws on methodological choices.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss measurements or power-law fits in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No extrapolation from small-run loss fits to larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or comparison of parameter and token growth.
No controlled comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning scaling laws, or transfer scaling laws are tested.
Tests accuracy on adjective–noun compositional tasks across model sizes, but not pretraining loss, broad downstream task suites, or a quantitative prediction rule.
No scaling-law exponents, fitting choices, or curve bending are examined.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: ANTAILS, larger checkpoints compared with base models
reader_labels.reason: Both reported ANTAILS setups show higher accuracy for the larger checkpoint in each of the four model families (A3, A6, A9, A12, A15, A18, A21, A24); the Mixtral increases are small.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: COMPCOMB, larger Falcon, Llama, and CodeLlama checkpoints
reader_labels.reason: The larger checkpoints have higher reported accuracy for both representation settings in these comparisons (C5, C6, C11, C12, C17, C18).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: PLANE, CodeLlama size comparisons across adjective classes and setups
reader_labels.reason: The larger CodeLlama checkpoint improves on subsective cases but is lower on intersective and intensional cases (P2, P4, P6, P8, P10, P12); the paper also reports that the larger CodeLlama model is worse overall than the base in this dataset.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The embedding-layer accuracy decreases while the last-hidden-state accuracy increases (C23, C24), so the direction depends on representation.
